title: Tabletop Battles Recaps: Codex Adeptus Custodes 11th Edition
content:
Today's the day the actual Codex Adeptus Custodes book releases in full, so we thought we'd recapitulate the work our team has done since embargo as a read-along guide now that the book's in your hands. First, our review of the Codex itself:

  • Tabletop Battles Reviews: Codex Adeptus Custodes 11th Edition

That has all of our top-line thoughts on the army in 11th edition, the various new and changed rules for it, our takes on the Ka'tahs, Rob's irritation that he doesn't get to do five touchdown dances in a row and spike the ball in the endzone on Custodes players because this Codex is actually good; all that stuff. Then we've gone over the Detachments on offer for competitive play one by one:

And last weekend, after having some time to digest what they'd read (and argue about it constantly on Discord for the full week), the team sat down in a roundtable to hash out how they feel the Codex will perform on the table, and what concerns the book has given them moving forward both for the Adeptus Custodes themselves and the rest of 11th edition:

  • Roundtable: Codex Adeptus Custodes 11th Edition

We're done with new Codices for the year, but that doesn't mean our competitive 40K coverage is taking a break this holiday season; in addition to Ruleshammer on Friday and Competitive Innovations every Wednesday and Friday (and some Saturdays), stay tuned for more entries in our Lore to Table series, new Start Competing content, and three pieces of subscriber-only 40K writing from top players in the current game every week!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. title: Tabletop Battles Reviews Tenebris Somnia
content:
Arriving just in time for the last half of October, New Blood dropped the finalized version of the vaulted "FMV Survival Horror" Tenebris Somnia, teased quite a while back with a pretty impressive trailer and demo nearly two years ago. The game especially caught my eye because of New Blood itself, a publisher that's produced some of my favorite games in recent memory (Ultrakill, Fallen Aces, and FAITH), but it wasn't exactly explained how the game would combine the live-action FMV elements with the gameplay itself, which seemed to feature pixelated side-scrolling action. So when the game released earlier yesterday, I took advantage of some of the extra time I had on my hands to dive in. I figured if it didn't end up impressing me, I'd simply refund it, and if it was at least decent, I could maybe finish it over the weekend.

As I put this review together, it is currently 5:30 AM in my timezone, and I realize that I spent much of my day playing Tenebris Somnia, watching other people play Tenebris Somnia, taking a little break to do my household tasks while thinking about Tenebris Somnia, and then finally having felt that I digested the game enough, sat down to write a review about Tenebris Somnia.

The concept now of even having considered thinking of a refund is quaint.

Full Motion, Live Action, All Gas

To address perhaps the biggest thing the game made waves with, Tenebris Somnia features live action cutscenes that are primarily acted out without voice acting; while not exactly silent films, the music, sound effects, and the occasional panicked noise or gasp or growl is all that fills the space. The initial "FMV" tag was something that I think stands out as something I'm not entirely sure I'm sure is the correct tag to use, but also there really aren't many other proper ways to use them. For example, the famous trailer footage used of the demonic presence lunging at our protagonist, Julia, and in the game you'll see that same scene as well as quite a few others. The issue I've had as I sat on the concept is thinking back to FMV games like the absolutely abysmal Night Trap or the amazing X-Files game for the PS1, among many others: the FMV aspect isn't directly involved in the gameplay, but instead takes the place of cut scenes and important plot points for the game. I don't think it is wrong to call it FMV, but if you're thinking of FMV games like the above mentioned adventure/point and click style, there's a bit of a difference here.

That said, the live action scenes are amazing. The acting and cinematography show some very fun craft and consideration of how to represent the ideas or concepts without relying on dialogue, but as practical effects fan, I really have to applaud the team here for what they've managed to put together; there are some truly gnarly practical effects throughout the game that blew me away when they occurred, and I don't really want to spoil them but let's just say that the monster reveals get increasingly awesome and intricate as the game progresses, with their FMVs really selling them; the endings also make really great use of the live action juxtaposition (there are 4 endings, by the way), and by the time I was done with the game I had really come around on the mixture of pixel art gameplay and live-action horror.

Surviving the Horrors

The actual gameplay of Tenebris Somnia is that of a survival horror game, played out entirely in 2D; you can move Julia along the cardinal directions (which is to say, up, down, left, and right) in the scenes in which you control her, but there is really only the flat 2D plane of the game. You'll be doing a fair bit of backtracking in the game, as the somewhat restricted environment also plays into survival horror expectations; instead of a police station or rural, foggy city, Julia spends the game exploring a twisted version of her ex's memories, primarily taking place at a film school.

Something I found fairly of interest early on is that the game does have a fair amount of written dialogue and terminology that tells the story of what is actually going on in this alternative reality and the mystery of Julia's ex (and her own issues), but there isn't a lot of reading required to complete the game, instead often having objectives explained through visual and color cues. I know it is an odd thing to praise a game for, perhaps, but I enjoyed that the game did not rely on huge flashing signs going DO THING HERE, while instead letting the visual language and storytelling do the work and hoping the player can piece things together.

Like most survival horror games, the main gameplay loop comes down to exploration and combat, and puzzle solving. I will say that puzzles were the weakest overall aspect of the game, because many of them were simply "find a symbol/locked door/etc, find the thing that matches that, open/solve/move past the obstacle". There are some pretty fun puzzles that play into the focus on film and movies that the game has going on in the background of its concept, but overall the puzzles mostly exist to give the game something to have you "do" to excuse the back and forth exploration.

Perhaps the surprise here for me is that the combat was the star. A 2D survival horror game with good combat? I have to give that a lot more thought than I have time for at the moment to whether or not I can think of a similar experience, and frankly, survival horror game combat is often not the star of the show. At some level, it is a little funny that Julia can so easily tackle all of the horrible beasts you encounter in the game, but also, it feels pretty good and controls well, allowing even for melee combat to feel less like a last resort and more like a viable option whether or not you are running low on ammo. This especially shines in the boss fights, all of which I frankly found to be a lot of fun and quite imaginative, making great use of the vibe and concepts of the game to present the bosses as fun, challenging, but never frustrating.

Absolute Cinema

I mentioned that film and movies play a big role in Tenebris Somnia, and I wanted to touch on that in a way that won't spoil the game at all; I often find that horror games are best experienced without really knowing the plot beforehand (and perhaps that can be said of just about anything with a plot, but I digress) simply because most of the time the mystery, suspense, and conceits of horror games are wrapped up in their stories. I think perhaps no series has suffered this violence of being spoilered to hell and back than Silent Hill, and Tenebris Somnia certainly has some influence and nods to that series here that makes going in with little information valuable. Primarily, it makes playing the game again, or replaying certain scenes or attempting different endings, more meaningful; you start to notice the concepts and ideas the game was sprinkling in the whole time after your initial experience, rather than having had some loudmouth tell you them all in advance.

In that way, it's pretty clear that the team on Tenebris Somnia love movies, as if the lovingly made and weird practical effects scenes weren't key enough. But there is a lot of focus on what movies are, and what they mean, and how they are made, that permeates the game and its narrative; in a lot of ways, it tends to do so both directly and subconsciously, working in concepts of perspective, storytelling, editing, and the like into the narrative of the game (as in, what Julia is experiencing) and as a story told between the developers and their audience, who are playing and watching Julia's story. While there's always a common discussion going on between the relationship of video game and film and how they influence, react with, or even at times fight for relevance against one another, Tenebris Somnia isn't super interested in that; it seems more interested in exploring the concepts of the viewer and the viewed, and the story it wants to tell resonates with that as well. Perhaps the thing I liked about the game, aside from one of the endings which I found very fun, is that it tells a solid narrative that takes full effect of the mixed media of the game itself. Julia is a solid protagonist, and I liked playing as her as much as I liked watching her, and I found that both the "game" Julia and "movie" Julia felt coherent.

If you're in the mood for a fun new horror game to play as we move closer to Halloween, or just enjoy survival horror and fascinating indie games that take advantage of their gimmick and aesthetic to the max, then Tenebris Somnia is a very solid recommendation; I found it took me about 8 hours to fully see everything the game had to offer, but I actually think I may play through it fully again after I get some sleep and rest on the game; it's a lot of fun to play, and I'm curious to see people talking about it following the initial release wave; if you end up picking the game up, I'd love to hear your thoughts on it!

title: [40K] Competitive Innovations in 11th: Assault Phase pt.3
content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

Well well well, if it isn't more Warhammer. Fancy finding that here. Fewer Marines today - as sometimes happens, the sorting algorithm randomly crammed them into the first two parts, so there's a bit of a broader field today. Wonderful.

Archetype

Extreme Devastation

Thoughts

Marshall continues the Necron theme he's been exploring this year, which is how best to use the high-volume shooting to obliterate foes. This build is, somehow, even more all-in on that plan than his previous attempts, bringing both terrifying turbo-buffed gauss volleys from Immortals and three different sources of massed Devastating Wounds to combo with Synergistic Empowerment out of Cryptek Conclave. That will annihilate pretty much any Infantry target you care to point them at (and hey, there's a lot of those right now), while the stacked output of all the Immortals can flense enemy vehicles to death. On top of that, there's a legitimately huge number of bodies here, and it can be very hard for foes to put down fast enough to avoid the grind, especially with Fall Back/Shoot on all the Immortals from the Wardens. As a last thing, the build also plays Priority Assets super well, having cheap tools for early scoring and a lot of ways to put plenty of OC on a point to get the final actions over the line. Very unique, very cool, congratulations Marshall!

Archetype

Cursed Herohammer

Thoughts

More Necrons in second place, this time on the popular Cursed/Skyshroud plan. Jacob's build leans especially hard to wards the herohammer angle, doubling up on C'tan, and only taking one unit of Lokhusts, spending lots of points on Skorpekh with Lords instead. I've definitely found the Skorpekh/Lord units to be a very neat little package, and love a bit of C'tanhammer, so this obviously appeals to me very much. Also intersting is the use of a Destroyer overlord just with 10 Warriors - not quite as punchy as Lychguard, but a lot cheaper, and great for maximising the value of the resurrection orb, and flipping points late game. This remains one of my very favourite archetypes to play, so I'm delighted to see it thriving in the wild, great stuff Jacob.

Instead, a big unit of Rubricae provides an additional threat alongside Magnus, a Vortex Prince and a Defiler. Thoughts

Heavy Librarius Ravenguard takes foes on one last whirlwind ride. A whirlwind ride of getting blown to bits by improbably chunky teleporting men, but a whirlwind nonetheless. Raven Guard are lagging a little bit behind their brethren with the new book, and it does feel a little bit like the terror of builds like this might have resulted in a slight overcorrection, but the new metagame is young, so I'm sure we'll see some tinkering as everyone switches to the new book. Archetype

Thoughts

AdMech get their go at a 12-stratagem build here, combining the powerful tools Cohort Cybernetica provides to Kastelans with a whole bunch of Skitarii buffs from Eradication Cohort. Robots are an extremely solid known quantity at this point - their current price is right, the detachment empowers them to really thrive, though not having the AoC from Lords hurts them a little. The trade-off there is pretty big, however - the Amplifier means they get to double dip on all the Skitarii tools from Cohort and Thulia, giving them extreme flexibility beyond even what they normally manage (and is also a good reason to go for the mixed melee/shooting build rather than double fist). Eradication also provides great support for various supporting pieces - the big Infiltrator unit can bury foes in charge mortals, the now very cheap Hastarii/Marshall units can blow Unshackled Wrath for big trade-ups, and even the non-Skitarii Destroyers can Fall Back/Shoot, removing their weakness to getting tagged. There's honestly just a massive amount of stuff here too, a lot for foes to try and push through, and the re-rolls on the Marshall units help it engage on multiple fronts better than many AdMech lists manage. This build looks really cool, and it's good to see Hastarii finally make some waves, congratulations Mr. Beef.

Thoughts

Shooty and Meganobz Orks face off against maximum Wyches for today's showdown, playing a mission combo that rewards skirmishing in the centre, and tabling the foe if at all possible. Looking at the lists, if I'm honest, this ends up feeling a little mis-matched. The Orks have build a bit wider than normal, which can absolutely help in some games, but absolutely does not here. Smaller pieces like the buggies are perfect for the Scourges to pick off, earning points into the bargain, and the chunkier stuff like the Dakkarigs risk suffering the same fate if they're not careful. Sure they're good at killing elves, but can they actually find a high-value target before they're blown up in turn?

Shooty Ork pieces do, also, have something of a vulnerabiltiy to getting tagged in combat, and that's bad news because this is an extremely "tag you in combat" sort of Drukhari build thanks to its speed and access to A Challenge Met. Because of the way scoring in this mission works, if one side has an angle on cautiously picking the foe apart, there's very little reason not to go for it, and I think the Drukhari have the perfect angle here. The Orks best counterplay is probably to be pushy with the Flash Gitz - they can't really be shot at without taking a whole unit with them, and have enough wounds that they'll soak a swing from most of the Drukhari unit (even Lelith won't take the whole squad out), and then can plausibly interupt and wipe whatever has multi-charged them. Time that alongside an Ingress from the big Meganobz unit (whose Armour of Contempt is very good here) and maybe that provides some momentum for the Orks, but it's tough going. As is, the Drukhari won in pretty confident style.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Age of Sigmar Khazalite Holds Battletome
content:
We’d like to thank Games Workshop for providing us with a review copy of this Battletome. We have also been provided with a provisional Battle Profile list for the army to use when writing the review, but please note that any points referenced in this review are subject to change until they are published on Warhammer Community.

For a few years now now, rumors have percolated about what exactly was going to be done with Fyreslayers. It’s an army with a very limited model range and seemingly very little enthusiasm to expand it. Much hay has been been made if they would be folded into Kharadron Overlords, or just removed entirely. Turns out there was a secret third option: A return of Dwarven Mountain Holds from Warhammer Fantasy, rolling the Fyreslayers into this larger force that helps expand their theming and grant a larger variety of playstyles.

The lack of a “traditional fantasy dwarf” has been felt pretty strongly in Age of Sigmar so this seems like a very exciting addition to the game. We got our hands on the new Battle Box with the Battletome included, so how do they stack up on the table? We’ve had a dozen or so test games under our belt and are here to report our findings.

Khazalite Holds Clanshields - Credit Mildnorman

Battle Traits

For Khazalite Holds the first thing that the army deals with are Grudge marks, each unit in the army gains a bonus effect for having Grudge marks on them. To gain them there are five ways:

  1. The first one is if your general is slain, you will hand out 1 Grudge Mark to up to 3 units.
  2. If a Grimmdron (aka Fyreslayers) unit charged this turn, did not destroy an enemy unit, and was not destroyed.
  3. If any Khazalite Hold units were slain that turn, hand out 1 Grudge Mark to a unit.
  4. If any damage points were allocated to your general, give one unit that is not your General a Grudge Mark.
  5. If any Krommdrom units are contesting an objective that is being contested by enemy units. Give a Grudge Mark

Next if an opponent gains control of an objective in your territory you can hand out one mark to a unit. Also, if a unit with a Grudge Mark retreats they lose a Grudge Mark. In your Hero Phase you can also have a unit count as having an additional Grudge Mark.

With some exceptions, Grudge Marks are binary, the unit only cares if you have them or you don’t. This kind of makes them read like a second pass at Demonic Power Points from Helsmiths, which isn’t an unwarranted comparison. Demonic Power Points required multiple to get anything out of them (often 3) and generated too slowly. This requires more interactivity to generate marks, but are more impactful out of the gate. It’s basically an army about deciding who needs to be buffed first and who can wait.

On top of the Grudge Marks, the army also has five Ancestral Vows they can activate once per game in any Hero phase. You can only activate one per round, and they last for the round, so it’s basically the successor to the Ur-Gold Runes from Fyreslayers.

  1. You can select an Infantry Hero and Infantry unit who are not in combat and wholly within 6” of the same piece of terrain, and remove them from the battlefield. Set them up wholly within 6” of a terrain feature outside 9” of enemy units.
  2. Pick 3 units and if they have not charged this battle round, reduce rend from combat attacks by 1.
  3. Pick 3 units and add 1 to the wound rolls of combat attacks made by the unit. If they are Grimmdron Infantry they gain First Strike when they charge, as well.
  4. For the rest of the Battle round friendly units have +1 to Casting and Chanting Rolls. While they are Wholly 12” of a Khazalite Wizard or Priest they gain a 4+ ward against spell, prayer, and abilities of manifestations.
  5. Finally, 3 Duardin Khazalite Hold units in combat roll a D3, then heal/return models equal to the roll and do that much damage to an enemy they are in combat with. If the unit is Valayan use a value of 3 instead of D3.

And lastly while your units are missing at least half of the models in the unit, add 1 to the attack characteristics of melee weapons used by the unit. Nice little perk for making sure your units are never truly out of the fight.

Battle Formations

War Callers subtracts 3 from the control scores of enemy units while they are in combat with friendly Khazalite units. This battle formation is great to have your army be able to take control of an objective that your opponent is trying to hold. With the General’s Handbook moving in a direction of Objective Control being the focus, having the ability to flip control is great.

Hearthsworn Defenders: Subtract one from hit rolls for shooting attacks that target friendly Khazalite Holds while they are wholly in friendly territory or while every model in the unit is contesting an objective you control. The ability to have your entire army be able to be minus one to hit in shooting is amazing. Khazalite Holds are an army that wants to fight in the middle and hold the objectives. Being able to be a little more survivable while your army treks up to the objectives is the way to go in my testing.

Unyielding Anvil: While an enemy unit is in combat with a friendly Khazalite unit, subtract 1” from pile in moves to a minimum of 1”. This battle formation is solid, the amount of times that the reduced pile in move actually matters in a game is non-zero, however either one of the previous battle formations I believe are better choices.

Wayfarer Nomads: When you declare a Run or Charge ability for a Khazalite unit and they are more that 6” away from all other friendly units, you can reroll the dice that determine how far it can move. This is probably the weakest of the bunch regarding the battle formations. As an army that has a decent amount of auras that you want to stay within. Forcing your army to social distance weakens the strength of it.

Heroic Traits

Long of Beard or Braid: Each time a visible friendly Khazalite unit wholly within 12” of this unit makes a Rally roll, you may make 3 additional rally rolls of d6. This is a solid choice, being able to rally your units on 9d6 is always good. Especially when a lot of your units are single wound models you can bring back huge chunks of a unit, if not the entire thing. Next there is Sworn to Vengeance which if the bearer’s non-Companion weapons allocates any damage points and the enemy unit was destroyed, you gain a vengeance token, to a maximum of 3. Until your next turn add 1 to the attack characteristics of non-Companion weapons of this unit. Out of the 3 options for heroic traits I think this is the weakest one. It is super situational and the other 2 traits are better options.

Finally Innate Resonance gives a non-priest Wizard(1). If it already has Wizard(1), it gains Wizard(2). In addition enemy manifestations strike last while they are within 12” of this unit. I think this is the one to take, being able to have a second wizard or even having your wizard be a 2 cast is great. With both spell lores being solid, the ability to cast another spell without having to take another model is great.

Artefacts of Power

Hearthflares: Pick an objective within 12” of this unit. Until the start of your next turn add 5 to the control scores of friendly units while they are contesting that objective. This to me is by far the best Artefact for the army. This allows you to overtake objectives very easily and it does a great job of allowing you to keep an objective flipped in your favor to deny your opponent from scoring what they would need to score the 10 points on primary.

Flamescale Rune Cloak subtracts 1 from hit rolls for attacks that target this unit if it has not charged this turn. This one is just fine, I just don’t think the army has a problem with survivability.

Finally, for the Deep-Earth Runic Weapon you select one of the bearer’s non-Companion weapons to be the runic weapon and add one to the rend characteristic. Then you can either get +1 to attack or take a gamble on getting +1 attack and damage on a 5+. Probably not worth it unless you’re a gambler, but fun if you are.

Spell Lore

This book has two spell lores which both are solid and a viable option. First we will cover the Resonance of the Runes. Up first is the Rune of Might casting value of a 6, until the start of your next turn add 1 rend to melee weapons used by friend Khazalite Holds who are within 3” of the caster. After that is Rune of Sanctuary, this spell on a casting value of 6 makes it so your army isn’t visible outside of 12” of enemy units. Nothing flashy in this spell, just a solid tool to allow you to move up the board without fear of being shot. The last spell in this lore goes off on a 6, and it is the Rune of Warding This creates an aura around the caster of 12” of enemy units can’t score critical hits. This is probably the strongest spell in this lore.

The next lore is the Reverberations of the Runes. This spell lore I think is a little weaker than the first one but still worth consideration. The Rune of Dismay, this spell subtracts 1 from the attack characteristics of melee weapons used by enemy units within 6” of the caster. The bubble that this emits is a little small to get a great use out of it, but it is really useful. Next up, Rune of Courage this spell emits an aura of reroll charges within 12” of the caster. This spell is useful, but you can just take the free manifestation of Aetherwrought and get this effect with the Cogs. The final spell in this lore goes off on an 8, and the Rune of the Furnace Will do d3 mortal wounds to all visible enemy units within 12” of the caster.

Prayer Lore

The prayer lore of Ancestor God Recitations is a fine one. However, there are no new models that are priests in the book, so you have to rely on the current crop of Fyreslayer Priests. First up is the Recitation to Valaya, this prayer goes off on a a 4+ and gives a unit -1 to be wounded which is great and the empowered version on a 8+ selects two units. After that we have the Recitation to Gazul which on a 4+ prevents manifestations from being set up within 12” of the caster. Which is nifty but that’s it. Just nifty. The final Prayer is a Recitation to Grimnir which picks an enemy unit within 18” on a 4+ everytime they do a Core ability they take 1 Mortal Wound. If the roll was a 10+ they take D3 instead. 

Endless Spells/Terrain

With the release of this book the army did not gain any terrain or manifestations. I would recommend using either Aetherwrought or Forbidden Power, as those are some of the more generally useful ones.

It is worth noting that the Fyreslayer Terrain and manifestations are still legal until they move to legends in the next year. Rules as written though, they don’t work because they proc off of the “Fyreslayers” keyword, which the book does not use anymore. So either they’ll change the warscrolls to word replace Fyreslayers with “Grimmdron” or just kill them entirely. If they do make them usable, though, the terrain is free so maybe worth it if you bring a priest.

Since Fyreslayers have a bit of weird synergy with each other, we’ll talk about them separately.

Khazalite Holds Hjulda Drakkblud - credit Bair

Heroes

High Kyng Valankrom, the named big boat does so much stuff. To start, this boat is a beater in combat with 6 attacks at rend 2 damage 3 and Crit (Mortals) and then 6 more attacks at rend 1 damage 2. As expected from a big centerpiece model it also comes with a ton of buffs Along with that it grants +2” move to Khazalite Holds wholly within 12” of it. Along with in your hero phase you select one of 3 abilities:
  • Give retreat and charge
  • Make an enemy unit maximum 1 objective control
  • Give your Wizards and Priests +1 to chant, casting, and banishment rolls

It also hands out a grudge mark and gives units Anti-charge (+1 rend). At the start of each battle round it can also pick an enemy hero within 18” and start accusing it of things. If the enemy hero accepts the accusations, your army gains +1 to hit against it. If they deny the accusations, they cannot use any commands until your next turn.

Thrynn on War Throne the unnamed boat variant is still a great combat piece at 12 attacks at rend 1 damage 2. With 6 of them being Crit (Mortals). When this unit charges it does a 3+ that many Mortal wounds to an enemy within 1” of it. Also When this unit moves it can select an Kromdon Infantry unit wholly within 6” and not in combat, remove it from the battlefield and set it back up wholly 6” of it when it finishes the move. Abilities of the boat are sort of  similar to the named one. They both have an ability that you choose one of three: it can grant +2” to move, it can select a friendly unit wholly within 12” and turn off weapon abilities other than Companion for attacks that target it, or it can pick an enemy hero and remove the ability of Guarded Hero from it. Just like the named boat it hands out anti charge +1 rend to units equal to Grudge Marks. However it also has a Charge phase ability to do D6 mortals on a 3+, which can be nice if you roll high. For the most part you probably want to take the named variant, as the effects are just generally better.

Thrynn is an unnamed hero who chain fights with another non-hero infantry Kromdon unit within their combat range. That infantry unit gains +1 to hit rolls. In addition this unit gets +1 attack for each friendly unit wholly within 6” of it to a maximum of 3.

Hjulda Drakkblud picks an enemy to be grudged during deployment and while the enemy unit is within 12” of them, she emits an aura of reroll charges wholly within 12”. If there is no Grudged enemy unit on the battlefield you add 3 to the Control scores of friendly Khazalite Hold units while they are wholly 12” of her. The great part of this ability is you can select a unit in reserves, so you can get the control buff even if its not dead. While she is in combat she also gives a non-Hero infantry unit +1 to hit if they are within her combat range. The last ability she has is a Hero Phase ability where she selects herself and 2 other non-hero infantry and on a 3+ ignore the first wound of each phase. If she has a Grudge Mark, no roll required.

Runewright is the generic foot wizard has +1 to unbind and banishment rolls while it has a Grudge Mark on it. In addition to that, after you successfully cast a spell you can attempt to extend the range of it by 3” by rolling equal to or greater than the cast value again. You can repeat this as often as you want, but if you fail a casting roll, the entire spell fizzles. This is done before your opponent attempts an unbind, so it might be worth if if you either aren’t going to be able to cast the spell without extending the range anyway, or if your roll technically passed the casting value but is low enough that it would be too easy to unbind.

Gotrek, the little murder dwarf is back. With 8 attacks (and +2 attack for each Hero or Monster he’s in combat with) on 2+/2+ rend 2 3dmg Crit(Mortal) he is adequately designed to be a hammer in the army. With being so angry that he now stands up on a 3+ the first time he dies, he is a little more survivable than before. He lost his fight twice, but in exchange can now be teleported. The one downside about Gotrek is that he does not benefit from Grudge Markers or Ancestral Vows (He doesn’t believe in such nonsense). That said he’s pretty resilient and killy on his own, so he might still be worth it.

Infantry

Your basic troop is the Clanshields, a 1 wound 10 man unit with a 4” move, 3+ save, and 2 attacks. Their attacks are 3s/4s(3+ with a grudge token), with anti-infantry. The biggest perk to these frontline units is the fact that if all of them are contesting an objective you control they reduce rend for combat attacks that target them by 1. Pair that with the ancestral vow that reduces rend if you don't charge, you have a seriously survivable unit.

The gunline unit has two different builds: first up is the Clangunners with Shotcannons. This unit has 12” range with 2 shots 3s/3s crit(auto-wound). After they shoot, they can select an enemy unit that had any damage allocated to it and on a 4+ (3+ If they don’t have Fly), subtract 1 from charge dice Alternatively they can be built as Clangunner with Rifles. These are 2 shots at 18” range on 3s/4s Rend 1 Damage 1. After they allocate damage on a 4+ you can halve the units move. You add 1 to the roll if they are a calvary unit, or add 2 if they are a monster. Of these 2 units I prefer the the Shotcannons since these work in either turn, being able to potentially give 2 units one less charge die is worth the 6” less range in my opinion.

The next units we have are the Valayan Guardians, which come with two different loadouts. First of them is the Valayan Guardians w/ Runic Halberds these are a unit of 5 ladies on a 4+ save and a 4+ ward. 2 attacks 3s/4s 2 rend 2 damage. These are the more combat focused version of the kit. Their ability allows them to charge as if they have fly. They have to end within ½ “ of an enemy model. If they pass over any models they inflict D3 mortal wounds to them. If they have a grudge token you can re-roll the charge.

On the defensive side of the kit. Valayan Guardians w/ Rune Axes and Shields. These emit a 6” aura of a 5+ ward to Infantry and non-Gholem War-machines while they have a grudge token. Also if they are in combat with an enemy unit that charged they get to roll a die for each enemy model in combat with them and on a 4+ inflict 1 mortal wound. This is a great unit to support the unit of Clanshields that is guarding your frontline. Them being a 3+ save and keeping the 4+ ward save that their aggressive counterpart has is a solid tech piece to hold those objectives. Having 3 attacks each 3s/4s rend 1, 1 damage. What they lack in combat profiles they make up for in the ability to do some serious mortal wound output.

War Machines

In keeping what you’d expect from a Duardin army, there are your fair share of Warmachines here. Gholems of Gazul are 3+ save and units of 3 with 5 wounds each. They are a serious melee threat at 3 attacks 4s/2s rend 2 3 damage and they reduce Wards by 1 for their swings. If that wasn’t enough, every combat phase they trigger an ability to try and crush the armor of an enemy unit in combat with them. You roll a die, if you roll equal to or higher than their save the enemy unit is -1 save for the rest of the turn. Before you roll, your opponent can choose to sidestep the swing, giving you -1 to the roll but they also get -1 to hit. This unit is great and the ability on their scroll is fun and flavorful.

Gholems of Valaya, the female Gholems, do 1 less damage than their male counter-part but they gain 1 extra attack each, so it balances out the profiles. These Gholems will hand out a Strike-Last on an enemy unit that charges them on a 3+ for the rest of the turn. In addition to that, when this unit dies it will hand out 1 grudge token to every friendly non-Gholem Valayan visible unit on the battlefield. I think these are a solid choice especially when you need some of the Valayan Guardians to be able to hand out a ward save. However, I don’t think there are enough Valayan keyworded units in the book to justify taking these. Oathkeeper Cannon having 3 shots at 24” that inflict D3+2 damage at rend 2, can put a serious dent into a unit. If they have a grudge token the shots gain Crit(2 hits). However the big thing that this cannon does, is in your shooting phase you select an enemy unit that had any damage allocated to it by it’s shooting attacks. On a 3+ you can select one of three options. You can either: 
  • Give Strike Last to the unit,
  • Reduce their rend by 1, or
  • Give your army the ability to score crits against the unit on 5+ while in melee for the turn.

Now, Stonebreaker Mortar this mortar shoots at 30” with 5 shots, however it’s only rend 1 and damage 2. But just like their cannon counterpart the mortar also gains Crit(2 hits) with a Grudge token and it has a select one ability: 

  • Reduce the control score for an enemy unit that took damage from it to 1.
  • Prevent the unit from being able to use Run abilities until your next turn. 
  • Select each enemy unit that is within 3” of the target and roll a bad D3 mortal wounds on them. 

The first two are solid abilities, and can deny your opponent an objective or the ability to complete battle tactics. These are a solid pick for any list, having the utility of their abilities from that far of a range puts a lot of pressure on your opponent on where they can go.

Khazalite Holds Gholems of Gazul - credit Bair

Fyreslayers

Since Fyreslayers (or Grimmdron as the book calls them now) are kind of a weird faction within the army, with their own synergies and support for each other, we decided to cover them separately.

First, the token new foot hero, Ormyr and Ashtongue. This model is a pretty punchy combat piece for the army. If they have a Grudge Mark, they can add +1 to companion attacks for units within 12” (so basically the Big Boats and Magmadroths) and it can give either a Magmadroth’s Mount attacks +1 to hit or a Flameseekers unit ignore negatives to hit, wound and control. A final cute trick is he can make himself totally hidden from all units outside of 6” on a 3+, but its both friend and foe so you may not want to use this every turn. He’s fine, but you really need to be running a Magmadroth heavy list to get much out of him.

Many of the units are quite similar (in some cases, worse) so assume they’re the same unless noted otherwise. Runefather on Magmadroth was tweaked slightly to give +1 attacks to non-Fyreslayers infantry if it has a grudge marker, while the Runefather foot version gets a 4+ Ward from its royal Retinue if it has a grudge marker (sadly, it lost the bonus to control it used to have).

As for his son, the Runeson on Magmadroth lost his nitpicky monster centric abilities and got a new suite of abilities. He can transport a unit of Fyreslayer infantry like the Kharadron boats can, which honestly is pretty welcome for the 4” moving infantry. He also gets a horde clearer in the charge phase, rolling dice equal to the enemy unit size, and dealing mortals on a 5+. The foot version of the Runeson got a slight buff to its charge bonus, giving +1 to any Khazalite infantry or +2 if it has a grudge mark. He also got a twist on the chain fighting, where he doesn’t necessarily need to swing first, he can swing after another infantry unit instead and get the +1 to hit. It’s a lot less clunky in certain situations, and can help if you’re carrying a heroic trait or artefact that you’d rather he get the +1 to hit for.

Next is the Priests, the thing you’re liable to take even if you’re not all that interested in Fyreslayers as a whole, since they’re your only priests. The Auric Runesmiter on Magmadroth is basically the same, with a slight update to let it give its +1 to wound to any Khazalite unit if it’s got a grudge marker. The foot Runesmiter probably took one of the bigger hits, since it lost its deep strike ability. It can give +2” to move to a Fyreslayers infantry unit, and gets +1 to cast with a grudge marker. It’s fine, and since its your only priest its probably the one you’ll take anyway, otherwise you’re taking nothing.

Rounding things off with the miscellaneous Foot Heroes who survived, the Auric Flamekeeper got a bit of an upgrade on his pretty bad ability. It hands out the same buffs as before if you roll less than the number of destroyed units, but it does include all Khazalite units now and a 1 always works, so you might be able to get it on turn 1, even. It also gets -2 to the roll if it has a grudge marker, so it’s way more consistent. Grimnir’s Resolve in the Masterflame Rune is now reroll charge rolls instead of +1, which is a much nicer buff. He also hands out a grudge marker to every Fyreslayer within 6” if he dies, so your opponent has to choose between dealing with the Masterflame Rune or giving all your Fyreslayers a grudge token. Grimhold Exile got a once per battle teleport, Strike First if he’s outside of 6” of all other friendly units and a free D6” movement in the movement phase, even into combat. It’s a cute trick, but his damage profile is still just kinda mediocre which makes him difficult to recommend.

Onto the Infantry, Vulkyn Flameseekers got more anti-Monster tools, which might be useful in this monster heavy season. Drothmasters is now a flat 2 instead of D3, but with a grudge mark they can cause -2 to attacks on Monsters and shut off Rampages. Auric Hearthuard lost their ability to reduce movement characteristics, which will probably ruin them being taken, even if their new ability to cause -1 to hit isn’t bad. Finally, Hearthguard Berzerkers were compressed into one warscroll, mostly to their detriment since it means they didn’t get to keep Crit (Mortals), like the Grimhold Exile it gets a free D6” move in the movement phase, even right into combat. This could make them an interesting tech piece up front, to lock down enemy units before they can charge into you

We feel that, mostly, the Fyreslayers in the book got worse. They’re locked in a bit of a closed environment that makes them struggle to play well with others (the Runesmiter aside) and many lost the things that made them top the charts this past season. If you want to use Fyreslayers, you kinda have to lean heavy on them to get much out of their synergies.

How They’ll Play

When reading through this book, it seems like you want to create a force that sort of pushes up the board in a “death-ball” style. You have a lot of auras that your army wants to stay within. You’re going to push up the board and with all the Objective control manipulation that you can generate in the army. You will overtake the primary and then be survivable enough to prevent your opponent from reclaiming them. Each of these units when played has the potential to give some serious output and be able to out-grind most armies over the course of the game for a victory.

Overall this army has a lot of interesting gameplay, but I think that it’s going to focus more on a defensive style by controlling the primary. With the War Callers subfaction, enemy units face -3 OC when they are in combat with you. Combine this with the Hearthflares artefact that gives your unit +5 OC you have a lot of ways of controlling the objectives. On top of that you bring a cannon with you, now you can give a strike last, you have the option of the Gholems that can give a -1 to save and make your opponent -1 to hit, shock gunners will give -1 charge die. After putting the clan shields on objectives they become a seriously tough front line unit to deal with. After you place some debuffs on your enemy’s army, you really have a force that is going to be able to control the battlefield.

Armies of Renown

You get a whopping three Armies of Renown, and seemingly learning their lesson from Helsmiths, they did retain some way to get Grudge Tokens as part of their Battle Traits, since every unit relies on them to reach their full potential.

Valankrom’s War Throng

The “high concept” of this army is Valankrom’s personal retinue, you can include most of the army, just stopping shy of the Fyreslayer units:

  • High Kyng Valankrom (must be included)
  • Any Gholem unit
  • Any Kromdron unit

Essentially how the army works is Kyng Valankrom gets to pick D3 enemy units he can see in deployment and mark them as wrongdoers and then pick one within 12” each one of your Hero Phases. He also gets to do this at the end of any turn to a unit they inflicted damage on him. Being in combat with a Wrongdoer counts as having a Grudge Token, and its the chief way to (at least count as) having Grudge Tokens, so this shifts the playstyle from a more anvil style of play, where you are handing out Grudge Tokens in the base army, to picking enemy units that are vulnerable and striking out against them.

This unfortunately means ranged units are at a huge disadvantage, so once per battle you can target a unit and shoot them as if they had a grudge marker, but it has to target a wrongdoer. Finally if Valankrom dies, everyone gets +1 to attack for the rest of the battle. This is still not ideal since you need him to label wrongdoers, but if the battle is almost over, this might help you at least close the deal.

It gets a wholly unique spell lore, which is neat. The unlimited spell Rune of Vigour gives +2” of movement, while Rune of Banishment subtracts 1 from casting rolls and lets you banish manifestations on a 3D6 when within 12”, and Rune of Upheaval makes enemy units fail commands on a 6+ within 12”. All 3 encourage moving up the field quicker to make the most use of them.

Overall it’s…an interesting concept but definitely way less powerful than just playing the base army.

Fyrd of Fyrepeak

The first of the more interesting Armies of Renown, this is for people who have an ample Fyreslayer collection to have something to play while they build up their new, more diverse Duardin force. Here you can include any Grimmdron unit and that’s it, that’s the only requirement.

As you’re probably expecting, the battle traits here revolve around Ur-Gold Runes. Going back to the third edition tome (minus the 6+ amplified version part), these are all in either player’s Hero phase again, and last the entire battle round. Like before you only get one per round and they’re only usable once per game each. Putting it in the Hero phase is probably for the best so you don’t forget what you’re doing and can plan your turn ahead, though it can be rough to have to plan for a charge phase or combat phase that ultimately does not pan out like you hoped.

The Runes are all brand new, and include:

Rune of Fortune: Only hit by shooting attacks on 5s or 6s. Good opener, particularly against shooting armies.

Rune of Spellbreaking: Subtract 2 from enemy Casting and Chanting Rolls, while you get +1 to chanting. Another good opener, but you might save it for a key combat turn as well, depending on what spells they have.

Rune of Guarding: Ignore first point of damage each phase. It’s fine.

Rune of Speed: Re-roll run and charge rolls. Probably good round 1 or 2, right before a big mega charge.

Rune of Striking: +1 to hit and wound rolls. Not as flashy as Crit Mortals, but still nasty.

They also get Grudge points for killing a unit, so you're encouraged to push up the board early and start clearing away units. Their Heroic Trait Foeseeker also grants a grudge point to everyone in the army if you kill a marked enemy Hero with the bearer of the trait (or a consolation prize of everyone wholly within 12” if they didn’t do the deed).

Like Valankrom’s War Throng, they have a unique lore, but it’s a prayer lore, naturally.

Grimnir’s Protection gives a 5+ Ward (to 2 units when charged), Grimnir’s Fury is a horde clearer which does mortals on 5+s (4+s if supercharged) which is above average for this type of ability and finally Grimnir’s Geyser gives back the deep strike the Runesmith lost.

Overall I’d classify this as “Cute”. The intent and concept is clear, Fyreslayers players get to keep their Fyreslayers, but it’s probably not going to last long term as the limited ability options and the pared down Fyreslayer unit selection is a real hindrance.

Throngakor Alliance

Easily the most intriguing of the three, instead of restriction choices this expands them. This is the second Army of Renown since Legion of the First Prince to integrate units from another book. While that limited your options to a very select few, this opens up the entire Khazalite Holds book alongside the Kharadron Overlords book.

First, at the start of each battle round you trigger Stone and Sky where you choose a non Hero infantry unit from each army and as long as they are within ½” of each other they are -1 to wound rolls against them and have the Stone and Sky keyword (This does a few things with other abilities). ½” feels a bit harsh, feels like maybe should have been combat range, but it is what it is.

So what does this keyword do? First, Duardin Pride gives all units wholly within 12” of a Stone and Sky unit +10 Control which is a good start. If an enemy unit within 12” of a Stone and Sky unit uses a command, you get to hand out a Grudge point once per round. You can technically give these to Kharadron units, but it won’t do anything.

The keyword is also defined but what it does not do. With Hammer and Anvil you can pick a non-Stone and Sky unit that is in combat, and then pick a unit from the opposite faction (e.g. if a Khazalite unit is in combat, pick a Kharadron Unit) to shoot them and get Crit (2 Hits). Not a bad perk. The Vice also lets you pick a Friendly Khazalite Unit and a Friendly Kharadron unit in combat to give them both Crit Mortals which feels like an insane deal.

A small little perk as well is the straightforwardly named Transport Duardin which simply adds an addendum to let Khazalites be transported by Skyvessels as if they were Kharadrons.

The Spell and Prayer lores all key off of using a mix of units as well. The spells Rune of Spirit and Rune of Defence give +2” of movement -1 to be hit, respectively, within 12” of the caster as long as they have both a Kharadron and Khazalite unit near them. The sole Prayer lore lets you target an enemy unit, giving them -1 to attack when in combat with a unit of both factions.

Overall, neat idea. I’m not sure if it’s worth some of the tradeoffs, however. Grudge generation basically comes to a standstill and while Kharadrons don't care about that, the Khazalites certainly do which will impact their effectiveness and I don’t know that Kharadrons add much to their already pretty solid roster of units, except for maybe transport ships.

Regiments of Renown

Two Regiments of Renown, both are available to any Order army. As a side note worth mentioning, unless they invalidate it, Gotrek does remain as his own Regiment of Renown, just because he’s not here doesn’t mean it is invalidated and the new and improved version of him is probably very likely to see play unless it is just removed outright.

Fjori’s Vengeance

The Fyreslayers regiment, it contains:

  • 1 Grimhold Exile
  • 1 Auric Flamekeeper
  • 1 Heartguard Berzerker unit with 5 models

The regiment ability basically allows the Grimhold Exile to take his other units with him when he teleports, though he works best alone so you’ll want to split him up as soon as possible after landing. One unit then gets a Grudge Mark, you choose so do what you want.

Kinda lackluster, only gets one grudge mark and probably only useful if you really need a teleporting hammer.

Thengin’s Grudgesettlers

A chonker of a regiment, it contains:

  • 1 Runewright
  • 1 Clanshields with 10 models
  • 1 Oathkeeper Cannon
  • 1 Clangunners with Rifles with 10 models

This is a pretty expensive unit to drop in, but what makes it interesting is every unit in the army starts with a Grudge Marker and only loses it once they kill an enemy unit, which makes them an interesting sort of Blitz unit, they’re stronger in the early game before they’ve killed stuff, so you can use them to try and take out key pieces early while the rest of your army marches up. That said, it is pretty expensive and hard to recommend for that reason.

Final Thoughts

New armies are always exciting since they bring a huge dynamic shift to the game. They can be difficult to predict, since we don’t have as much information to go on as an updated version of an older book, but we’re pretty confident that this is a strong book.

It is very technical, with a high skill floor where minor mistakes might cost the game, but under a skilled hand it’ll probably win a lot of games. Some of the attacks we’ve been able to dish out in test games are absolutely eye watering and it’ll be exciting to see what people do with it.

This may not have been the army Fyreslayers players we’re hoping for, but it’s a pretty damn interesting one.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Age of Sigmar Khazalite Holds Army Box Miniatures
content:
The Khazalite Holds have arrived, and Norman and Bair are taking a look at the army set. Our thanks to Games Workshop for providing Goonhammer with review copies.

A year after the release of the Helsmiths of Hashut, we have some new duardin on the block with the release of the Khazalite Holds. It's somewhat odd these guys are brand new, as they’re the most generic dwarf type army we’ve gotten in the setting and feel a bit like coming home, but that’s not to say its unwelcome. If you’re looking for heavy armor and a habit for grudging, look no further because the Khazalites are for you.

First Impressions

Norman: The box set is much what you’d expect, you get the models (obviously), a limited edition Battletome with some pretty sick cover art, and the faction cards which I personally have still never really had a use for but I’m sure some sickos out there are excited to get. One weird quirk with this box set is that the instructions only let you build the variants for the Spearhead (boy type Gholems and cannon instead of girl type Gholems and mortar). You can find the instructions for those builds on Warhammer Community, but it's a bit odd not to get them.

Bair: I built all of these before WarCom put up the instruction PDF and did not feel like getting creative either. Norman covered the rest already, it's an army box like you've come to expect for a new army release. I like that it's a Spearhead straight out the box giving you something to start playing with immediately too until the rest of the army comes out, pretty smart move there.

The Models

Khazalite Holds Hjulda Drakkblud - credit Bair

Hjulda Drakkblud

Bair: She sure is a named character foot hero model. That's to say that there aren't any options whatsoever in the kit, which is fine really since you're just buying the army box once anyways and being patient for the kits to come out separately. She goes together really well and I was happy that the cape is all one piece instead of the weird splits that can happen in minis sometimes that can cause weird splits in them to glue together. Virtually no mould lines to clean off and a real joy of a mini to paint to boot! I like the Dragon/Magmadroth scale cloak that sits on top of the normal cloth cape on her back, a really nice tie-in detail.

Oathkeeper Cannon

Norman: Unfortunately I only had time to build this kit and not paint it, but I have some thoughts on the build. The build itself is fine, there are some nasty seams along the length of the cannon if you’re not careful but it's nothing that can’t be solved through the use of some sprue goo. Much like its Helsmith counterpart, the base has a little diorama of the crew loading and firing the cannon. While this is neat, it can be a bit daunting that you have to paint three characters along with the cannon itself as just set dressing. They aren’t simple asks either, there’s one guy grabbing a rune from the fire, another firing the cannon, and a woman making ammo out of some rocks (had to look this up in the book). It's far from impossible and a treat to do the first time, but I can see this getting daunting if you end up wanting to run multiples of these.

Khazalite Holds Oathkeeper Cannon

Khazalite Holds Oathkeeper Cannon

Bair: I, too, did not get time to paint it but found the build the be real easy overall. There's a bit of awkwardness with the crew and spacing them all out correctly, the smith apprentice guy feels a little cramped, but that's about it. The only "real" complaint I have is the lack of variation and options in the crew so if you want multiple without looking the same you'll want to do some conversion work with other kits.

Khazalite Holds Gholems of Gazul - credit Bair

Gholems of Gazul

Norman: These kinda sucked to build honestly. For one, none of the pieces you need are near each other, which makes every step mean you have to look across three sprues for what you need. On top of that, there are some weird sub builds on these, like having to build the neck and the legs and feet being multiple pieces. There are a ton of options here though, letting you fully customize your constructs to fit your army. I wish there was a bit more variability with the poses, but at least for big stone guys they’re a bit dynamic.

Bair: I didn't mind the build on these so much actually but they're definitely not intuitive with three parts per foot and parts spread across each sprue instead of being next to each other. I put these together before Warhammer Community put out the PDF and the instructions in the box only have the ones for the Gazul version so that's what I built. Lining up the two handed hammers was easy enough and they joints lock into place to make it nearly idiot proof.

Clanshields

Khazalite Holds Clanshields - Credit Mildnorman

Norman: On the build side these guys are pretty straightforward, barring two interesting quirks. First, you can build your standard bearer and musician off two different models, meaning you can get some nice variance when you inevitably have to build 40 of these. The second is while there are a ton of options here, they aren’t labelled in the best way. The shields are straight forward but the heads are looking in different directions based on where the socket sits and it can make certain poses look off when your dwarf is looking in the opposite direction of the horn he’s posed to blow. Speaking of the heads, I wish the female heads looked a bit better here. The shawls they wear frame their head weirdly, and only one has any hair showing which helps break things up significantly. 

On the painting side, I tried to paint these well but as quickly as I could to see how much I could get away with. These models are mostly armor, so I decided to prime silver. While I don’t regret this course, it was a pain in the ass to paint over. There’s also a lot of leather on these models, which in combination with the beards that are everywhere, you’re gonna probably want a bit of variety in the browns you’re bringing to the table. The details themselves are pretty easy, with nothing on these models being a particularly difficult task. That is until you get to the banner. Unlike the Helsmiths there are no transfers for these guys. The banners are big wide open canvases that will work very odd with nothing on them, so you’re gonna have to get comfortable with freehand. Luckily there’s some good references in the Battletome for the different runes the Khazalites use, all of which are relatively simple geometric shapes. Beyond the banner though, these paint up pretty quickly for a modern GW kit.

Khazalite Holds Clanshields

Bair: Just wanted to add here that you get 20 shields in total and 20 heads in total for the kit of 10 models; you get 10 of the same shield with the mountain symbol and then 10 shields with random runs on them, 15 male heads and 5 female heads in total. I agree with Norman that the female heads could be better, I really like the long braids that Hjulda and the one head in this kit have going on and would have loved to see more in that style!

Final Thoughts

Norman: This is a good set of models! As you can see in our review, a lot of them are useful too which is always a plus. With a named character in the mix, you probably won’t be doubling up on these, but clanshields and the cannon will be in all my lists most likely and I’m sure I’ll find a spot for the Gholems. I’m really looking forward to seeing the rest of the range and building out this force.

Bair: Good dwarfs. I don't care much for the official scheme and think that photos can be a difficult medium to show new minis off in. Are these as good as the golden age of dwarf sculpts (6th Edition WHFB sculpted by Colin Dixon)? No, they're not, those hold a special place in my heart but I do really like these and am very glad to see "regular" dwarfs in Age of Sigmar. Finally, an army for me.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@goonhammer.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don’t forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website and more.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews Warhammer 40k Battlefields: Armageddon
content:
In this review we’ll be looking at the upcoming Battlefields: Armageddon boxed set for Warhammer 40,000, a box designed to give players a full table of painted terrain. We’d like to thank Games Workshop for providing us with preview copies of the box for review purposes.

One of the big reveals from Games Workshop at the Adepticon preview - before 11th edition even launched - was the release of a set of pre-painted terrain. Although not the first time GW have released pre-painted terrain - that honour goes to the Chapel of Sanctuary, released back in 2003 - the new set is arguably their most ambitious release in years, and certainly the first time they’ve offered a full “battlefield in a box” product that promised to be playable completely out of the box, no painting required.

Chapel Of Sanctuary

Attendees of GW’s 11th edition events this year will no doubt already be familiar with the assembled contents of these kits - Games Workshop have been eager to show them off at said events, allowing players to see firsthand how they look on full tables. What we haven’t seen to date however, is the assembly process for them, and how it differs, if at all, from the set of unpainted terrain GW released as part of their Starter Set product back in August.

What's in the Box

You get two full pre-painted sets of terrain. These are identical to the ones in the Starter Set, with identical packaging and sprues. The difference here is that the terrain has already been painted on the sprue. In addition to that terrain a set of the terrain footprints which are already available separately, and a set of "game mat boards" you can unfold to make a full 44"x60" table. Anyone familiar with existing GW boards or Kill Team will be familiar with these. They're thick and relatively heavy, and make up like half of the weight of this box, if not more.

Overall Impressions of the Terrain

TheChirurgeon: Generally speaking, this terrain set was a breeze to put together. It’s the exact same sprues as the unpainted kit from the Starter Set, but prepainted. This has one important knock-on effect, which is that the kit seems to have been designed with tolerances for the paint in mind. Everything here went together snugly and easily, no glue required - which was absolutely not true for the unpainted terrain. Compared to that kit, this was easier to assemble and stayed together much better.

The terrain has all been painted on sprue, and as a result you're going to have some gates and mold lines to deal with. For the most part, these are in decent places - only a couple were outright annoying or in spots I felt desperately needed a touch-up - but I also didn't feel like it was crucial to get these cleaned up, either - the coloring on the plastic and the paint makes it easy to miss them when you have it all assembled on the table. That said, we'll be looking to color match them later.

The paint jobs on the kit are, simply put, amazing. GW have done an impressive job capturing the ‘Eavy Metal paintjob on this terrain set, and the level of detail here is staggering. I’ve done a fair bit of terrain painting in my day, and suffice to say that there are details here I simply would not have bothered with if I’d been painting it myself. That said, the whole thing has a kind of "printed" effect to it - it's slightly grainy with a glossy/metallic sheen to it. I didn't have much issue with it but if it bothers you then I suspect giving the whole thing a coat of matte varnish will solve the problem.

This goes inside other pieces, and would have to be painted as a subassembly

This kit was absolutely designed to be pre-painted, and that was obvious back when we reviewed the unpainted version of the terrain box a couple of months ago. Pieces of this are absolutely set up to be painted before assembly, and I maintain that painting terrain with subassemblies is sicko shit. So much of the value here on this terrain is just how much work went into painting little details that I normally don't bother with when I paint terrain.

On that note, one of the nice touches here is the way the terrain is designed to go with the area bases included in the set. They match up aesthetically in a way that I find very pleasing.

All together, the whole thing looks great when you have it on a table. I'd be more than happy to play using this set, and I plan to, using it to replace most of my existing terrain. It's not that I don't love that terrain; it's just that the munitorum ruins end up being a bit too tall/wide for the 11th edition footprints. They make me think the board is less open and make it easier to hide - and I plan to expect worse.

Liam: Assembly-wise, this more or less goes together fine. I didn't have entirely the same experience as Rob; while it definitely fits more snugly than the unpainted version, glue was still required on some of the non-ruin pieces. I also found the plasma generator thing kind of a pain to put together, though I think I would have done myself a favour here by gluing each half together and then letting it set before carrying on. The paint is genuinely impressive. One of my favourite details is that the screens and plasma orbs have gloss finishes - it's seriously impressive stuff for a pre-paint and I would love more detail on the process. I can't imagine painting all of this myself - even with an airbrush it would be a serious time investment.

There are a couple of bum notes - as you probably guessed, the gates are pretty visible in places. There's some clever work done to hide them - the L shapes have a lot of them placed inside the join for example, so they're hidden away - but others are unavoidable. In some cases you just need to do a little bit of touching up, but a few of them are more difficult to fix, like the ones on the aforementioned plasma orbs. If you were desperate to scrape the mold lines off you'd create even more work for yourself.

That said, compared to painting the whole set, it's not the end of the world. The other issue is that in a few places I had parts that were simply not painted. The left edge of the taller barricades, for example, was pretty much bare on both sprues. I assume this is to do with how the manufacturing process works and you likely won't notice it in play, but it's worth mentioning that the process, while impressive, isn't flawless.

TheChirurgeon: For what it's worth, I don't think I had that issue in my sets.

Wings: I’m a dumb idiot who got very enthused about painting some of the ruins we got in the starter set, so I can provide a side-by-side comparison of what this looks like if you paint it yourself vs. get the pre-paints.

Credit: Wings

Credit: Wings

I guess the reassuring news given the time I poured into this is that I do think the one I painted looks slightly nicer. However. It does represent somewhere in the region of 6-8 hour’s work, whereas the pre-paint took me under five minutes to clip, tidy up, and assemble. I am not someone blessed with infinite spare time - if I was making a purchasing decision about which of these to get, I would obviously go for the pre-paints, they look good, they go together fast, and I’m hugely in favour of anything that lowers the barrier to entry for playing “real” 40K. I do, from examining my own paint job, think they missed a trick by not going for a brighter contrasting colour on the protruding metalwork on the ruin faces - doing that in the bright red really made mine pop, and something similar would look great on the pre-paints.

TheChirurgeon: Yeah I think the terrain easily compares to the stuff I hand painted. It has a lot more fine detail work than my paintjobs, where I'm letting washes do most of the heavy lifting. It's as good as the red Manufactorum terrain I painted, but probably not as nice as the paintjob on my white/gray terrain, and the Woodland Scenics greenery does a lot of heavy lifting there. The differences are easier to tell up close, and I think painted terrain has the edge in that department, but from above the table I don't think you notice much difference.

What's more important is that it looks great next to either of those, and great next to fully painted models. I'd be more than happy to have this all together on my table, and you're going to see it in a lot of battle reports moving forward.

Final Thoughts

Liam: For the price point, I think the product is great. It's high quality terrain with better paint on it than I would ever bother with, and you'll be playing games on a great-looking table faster than ever. I do kind of wish the card boards weren't included (the mats to make a playing surface, not the terrain areas). I've never liked these much as a product and I don't think I've ever known anyone to use them, though maybe they're more popular in groups where nobody wants to buy a separate mat. I understand the impulse towards having a battlefield in a box, though - this is a product they should have launched years ago. I'm interested to see if it remains a core stock item and is still available in say, 18 months' time. If it's successful I'd also love to see other spins on it with different aesthetics.

TheChirurgeon: Seconding the notion that I wish they'd left out the "mat" boards, as those are just fully extraneous at this point and the only part of this that's a legitimately bad product, especially compared to what else you can get on the market. I understand why it's in here but it adds a ton of weight and cost the kit didn't need. I agree that it's a solid value even at the MSRP of $395 in the United States, but if that price is giving you sticker shock, I'm not surprised. It's a big ask for a single purchase, even one you're going to use every game you play at home. That said, I think the terrain is just straight up worth having and I'd also love to see versions rocking different aesthetics. We've already seen slick MDF terrain mats at GW's events with snow and other themes for the terrain; I want to see those go up for sale with some appropriately themed terrain to follow.

title: TheChirurgeon's Road Through 2026, Part 43: Hobby Decisions for GN and WCW
content:
Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I talked about attending the 2026 Las Vegas Open, palling around Las Vegas with friends, and getting swept up in Gundams. This week it's mostly hobby progress - I spent the bulk of last week in NYC after Vegas, which usually crushes my ability to set up and play games on the following weekend.

Mostly this week I need to talk about hobby decisions. I have two major events coming up before the end of the year: The 2026 Grand Narrative and the 2026 World Championships of Warhammer. Both of those present relatively different goals/challenges for me, but aren't so wildly different in terms of what I'm hoping to accomplish.

The Grand Narrative

The Grand Narrative is always a fun time, and honestly one of the only events I really enjoy bringing my son to every year. A number of other Tabletop Battles authors will attend, and we tend to do lots of fun stuff together. We also started managing the event Discord last year, to rave reviews. With six games spaced out nicely over three days and little pressure on the games themselves, it's the kind of event I actually get to relax at a bit, and as Bryce has gotten older, he's been able to do his own thing there more and more.

As always, my plan is to win Best Painted at the event. I was gearing up to bring my Emperor's Children to the event, as I think they're a shoe-in if I can get them done in time but then well, they showed off the lore behind the event and the Lords of War for it. And now I unfortunately feel like I am compelled to bring my Red Corsairs, as any event in The Maelstrom involving a force being chased down by Huron's marauders feels like a perfect match for the army I spent the first quarter of the year building and painting. Plus, the army is already good enough to win Best Painted at an Event, and I can keep working on painting the army between now and the Grand Narrative to add quality models to it without having to go crazy. A little touch-up on my vehicles, maybe a display board upgrade, and I'm good to go here.

My current plan is to finish off some unfinished units in the force - a second unit of Red Corsairs Raiders, and add some interesting additional wrinkles. Namely a unit of Warp Talons made using Mk. III jump packs, some additional Terminators, and a unit of Chosen made using a mix of kits. The goal here is that every model should reflect the scavenged or post-Heresy aesthetic of marines who turned later on, using more Imperial aesthetics and going a bit less crazy on the trim and horns.

So I've been working on my Red Corsairs this week.

The World Championships

This is my stretch goal. I mentioned last week that I'm playing, and I went ahead and filled out the form and said "yeah, I'm going to this thing." Now I need to figure out what army I'm bringing. My goal right now is to go for Best Painted with Emperor's Children. That said, getting them there is a lot of work and I have a lot of models to paint if I want to get that done. The good news is that the new Tone Pro Paints help with that a bit - it's a faster time using them to get the scheme down, anyways.

If I can't get them done in time for the WCW, I'll just run my Red Corsairs - I think CSM suddenly have a lot more play with the Cabal of Chaos and the new strength/AP upgrades on combi-bolters, and I can run something that will be very solid using a lot of the existing models I have - I already have Huron and a Chaos Sorcerer and Terminators, and I can run the Fabius Bile + Chosen + Masters of the Maelstrom brick.

The goal right now for my Emperor's Children is to get cracking on the second Rhino, get that done, get a Defiler done, finish the unit of Noise Marines and the Lord Kakophonist, and finish my second unit of Infractors and another Lord Exultant. That won't give me a full army, but it'll put me around 1300 points, and I can figure out what's left from there and how I want to fill in the rest. Probably a unit of Flawless Blades to go with the Lucius I've already painted, and I'll see what else makes sense from there.

Other Hobby Progress

I'm more or less in a small holding pattern right now as I wait for the new Tone Pro Paints to drop this weekend. They're really good, but my current set has me feeling like I'm missing some key colors I'd like to play around with - specifically more of the pinks and reds. What I really like about the new paints is the way they kind of shade themselves - I can layer them over each other for smoother blending without having to do complicated wet blending like I usually do and that's a good help.

I noticed while doing updates on the World Eaters Detachment Focus articles this week that we had a dearth of newer World Eaters terminators painted, and so I've been working on fixing that problem as well, using one of the converted Terminators I did. I have a set of these and they were all pretty simple - just a pair of the Berzerker "ears" from an older 3E head/kit, and a necklace of skulls made by running a thin plasticard rod through a trio of skulls from the skulls basing kit. End result looks pretty much exactly how I wanted it to, mirroring the sick resin Forge World kits while still having the bulkier, more imposing frame of the new units. The shoulder pad is from the Eightbound/Exalted Eightbound kit.

The only shame of these guys is having to paint like ten or twenty of them to really get much out of them. That's asking a lot, and more than I'm willing to put in. But the effect here works. Compare this bad boy to the guys I painted back in like, 2017:

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

We've come a long way, baby. Though I do miss those kits - they looked amazing. I especially like the heads in them, and I may end up breaking the heads off those older kits to put on the newer kits if I do more conversions. They're just really good heads.

Final Thoughts

That's it for this week. My goal now is to get this stuff painted and get some practice games in, and start really prepping for Worlds in December. I need to play more games and get comfortable with whatever army I'm going to bring. CSM are relatively easy at this point; I've got a good handle on what I'd do with them. It's more the question of Emperor's Children, who I haven't really played since last year, but I've played against them enough to have a solid idea of what I'm doing.

See you Thursday.
